solution:
The correct alternative is (c).

Electromagnetic induction is the production of a current in a coil when the magnetic lines of force passing through it change, which is what happens when the coil and a magnet are moved relative to each other. The chapter introduces the effect with Faraday's demonstration: "In the year 1831 Faraday showed that an electric current can be produced in a conductor with the help of a moving magnet." It then states Faraday's law of induction: "whenever the number of magnetic lines of force passing through the coil changes, current is induced in the coil. This is known as Faraday's law of induction. The current produced in the coil is called the induced current."

The three other alternatives describe something else. Charging an electric conductor is a matter of static electricity and involves no magnetic field at all. The production of a magnetic field by a current flowing through a coil is the reverse relation — it is the magnetic effect of an electric current, in which a current already exists and a field results from it. The motion of the coil around the axle in an electric motor is again the reverse case: there a current is supplied to the coil and the resulting force makes it turn, so the motion is the effect of the current rather than the cause of it.

solution:
The correct alternative is (c) Electric Generator (DC).

Only a generator produces electricity. The chapter says of it: "Here, mechanical energy is used to rotate the current carrying coil in a magnetic field, around an axle, thereby producing electricity." An electric motor does the opposite job — it is "A device changing electrical energy into mechanical energy." A galvanometer and a voltmeter are measuring instruments; the chapter notes that a galvanometer "works on the same principle as that of an electric motor" and that "Voltmeter and Ammeter also work on the same principle", so they only indicate a current or a potential difference and generate nothing.

**Description of a DC generator.** A copper wire coil ABCD is kept between the two pole pieces of a magnet. The axle carrying the coil is rotated by a machine from outside, so the coil turns in the magnetic field and a current is induced in it, its direction being given by Fleming's right hand rule. As in the AC machine, the current in the coil itself reverses after every half rotation.

What makes the output direct is the ring on the axle. Instead of the two separate conducting rings used in the AC generator, "a split ring is fixed on the axle like a split ring used in electric motor. Because of this arrangement, the branch of the coil going upwards is always in contact with one brush and the branch going downwards is always in contact with the other brush. Hence, the current flows in one direction in the external circuit. This is why this generator is called as a DC generator." Two stationary carbon brushes press on the split ring and carry the current out to the external circuit, where a galvanometer or an ammeter shows it.

**Diagram.** Draw the coil ABCD between the N and S poles of the magnet, with the ends of the coil taken to the two halves of the split ring on the axle, the two carbon brushes touching the split ring from either side, and the external circuit containing the meter. Label the coil, the north and south poles, the split ring, the carbon brushes, the axle and the meter.

solution:
The correct alternative is (d).

In the chapter's experiment (fig 4.6) a thick copper wire is passed vertically through a piece of cardboard and a large current is sent through it. "the magnetic needle kept at different points on the cardboard around the wire stands in different directions", and when iron filings are sprinkled on the cardboard instead of the needle, "The iron filings arrange themselves in a circular manner around the wire." Since "The iron filings spread along the magnetic lines of force", the lines of force must themselves be circles drawn round the wire, lying in the plane of the cardboard — that is, in a plane perpendicular to the conductor, with the wire at their centre.

The chapter adds that the field weakens with distance: "If the current is unchanged, this magnetic field reduces as the distance from the wire increases. Therefore, the concentric circles representing the magnetic lines of force are shown bigger and rarefied as the distance from the wire increases."

The three other statements do not match this pattern. Two of them describe the lines of force as straight lines rather than as closed circles — in one case lying in a plane across the conductor, in the other running radially outward from it — but a straight or radial line would leave the iron filings pointing away from the wire, not curling round it. The remaining statement puts the lines of force parallel to the conductor, running along it on all sides, which would leave the filings lying lengthwise beside the wire rather than in circles.
